Lee-Carter model

Source: R/model-lee_carter.R
lee_carter.Rd

log m[x, t] = a[x] + b[x] k[t] with the constraints sum(b) = 1 and sum(k) = 0, fitted per stratum:

Usage

lee_carter(
  method = c("poisson", "svd"),
  jump_off = c("fitted", "observed", "filtered", "constrained"),
  bootstrap = FALSE,
  n_boot = 100,
  adjust = c("dt", "dxt", "e0", "none"),
  choose_period = FALSE,
  min_years = 20,
  rotate = FALSE,
  rotation = c(e0_start = 80, e0_end = 102, power = 0.5),
  family = c("poisson", "nb"),
  dispersion = c("global", "age"),
  jump_off_years = 1,
  seed = NULL
)

Arguments

method

"poisson" (maximum likelihood with the distribution of family) or "svd".

jump_off

"fitted" (forecasts start from the fitted rates of the last year), "observed" (from the observed rates of the last year; Lee and Miller 2001; with jump_off_years > 1 from their mean over the last years, Stoeldraijer et al. 2018), "filtered" (from the rates at the Kalman filter estimate of the index in the last year; De Jong and Tickle 2006) or "constrained" (the maximum likelihood fit is constrained to the observed rates of the last year, the forecast origin correction of Li, Hardy and Tan 2009; method = "poisson" only). See "Jump-off" above.

bootstrap

Semi-parametric bootstrap of the parameters.

n_boot

Number of bootstrap fits.

adjust

Re-estimation of k[t] for method = "svd": "dt", "dxt", "e0" or "none". With "dt", k[t] is the root of the total-deaths equation found by a search around the SVD index (package-specific: a bracket of k[t] +/- (10 + 10 |k[t]|), extended while the fitted total deaths do not cross the observed ones). A year where the search finds no root keeps the index of the SVD: a year without deaths has none, and with an age pattern b of both signs the fitted total deaths are not monotone in k[t] and the search fails in most years. A warning (class mt_warning_model_fit, in the diagnostics of the fit) names these years, which the fit of the stratum also holds (no_root_years).

choose_period

Choose the fitting period (Booth, Maindonald and Smith 2002).

min_years

choose_period considers fitting periods of more than min_years years (minperiod of demography::lca()).

rotate

Rotate the age pattern of decline b towards an ultimate pattern as life expectancy at birth rises (Li, Lee and Gerland 2013).

rotation

Settings of the rotation, a named vector: life expectancy at birth at which the rotation starts (e0_start, default 80) and is complete (e0_end, default 102), and the exponent of the weights (power, default 0.5). The defaults are those of Li, Lee and Gerland (2013, eq. 2) and MortCast; elements left out keep their defaults.

family

Distribution of the deaths for method = "poisson": "poisson" (Brouhns, Denuit and Vermunt 2002) or "nb" (negative binomial; Delwarde, Denuit and Partrat 2007).

dispersion

Dispersion of the negative binomial deaths (family = "nb"): "global" (one for all ages; Delwarde, Denuit and Partrat 2007) or "age" (one per age group of the data; Li, Hardy and Tan 2009).

jump_off_years

For jump_off = "observed": the number of last observed years whose mean log rates give the jump-off rates (default 1, the last year; 2 to 5 in Stoeldraijer et al. 2018).

seed

Random seed of the bootstrap resamples (bootstrap = TRUE). The resamples of each stratum come from its own random number stream, and these streams start from seed, so two fits with the same seed have the same bootstrap parameters with any number of cores. NULL (default): the streams start from the current generator (set.seed()). The forecast draws have their own seed in mt_forecast().

Value

A model specification.

Details

  • method = "poisson": Poisson log-bilinear model (Brouhns, Denuit and Vermunt 2002), maximum likelihood by Newton updates;

  • method = "svd": original method (Lee and Carter 1992): singular value decomposition of centred log rates, with k[t] re-estimated in a second stage (adjust, as in demography::lca()): so that the fitted deaths match the observed total deaths of each year ("dt", Lee and Carter 1992), by Poisson maximum likelihood of the deaths by age given a and b ("dxt", Booth, Maindonald and Smith 2002), so that the fitted life expectancy at the first age matches the observed one ("e0", Lee and Miller 2001), or not at all ("none").

choose_period = TRUE fits the model to the last years only, starting in the year that minimises the ratio of the mean deviance of a fit with a linear k[t] to the mean deviance of the Lee-Carter fit (Booth, Maindonald and Smith 2002): the longest recent period over which the decline was close to linear (demography::lca(chooseperiod = TRUE, breakmethod = "bms") gives the same period). Fitted rates of earlier years are missing.

Compared with demography::lca(), k[t] is centred again after the second stage (a constant shift of k and a, with identical fitted rates), and life tables use a_x = n/2 at age 0 (as life_table()), so adjust = "e0" matches a slightly different life expectancy than demography's life table where age 0 is in the data.

The period index follows a random walk with drift. Draws include the innovations and the uncertainty of the drift. With bootstrap = TRUE the parameters are re-estimated on n_boot Poisson resamples of the fitted deaths of the fitting period (semi-parametric bootstrap with fitted deaths of Renshaw and Haberman 2008), which adds the uncertainty of a and b. The bootstrap of Brouhns, Denuit and Van Keilegom (2005) resamples the observed deaths instead: bootstrapped(lee_carter(), type = "data") (bootstrapped()). A seed makes the resamples reproducible.

Age groups without deaths in the fitting period get a constant rate (0.5 deaths over the period) and no trend; with adjust = "e0" they enter the life tables at that rate.

Safeguards of this package for sparse counts. Where the Poisson likelihood has no finite maximum (method = "poisson" with very few deaths), the fit falls back to two package-specific estimators (reference unknown), each with a warning (class mt_warning_model_fit; within mt_fit() it is reported with the stratum): first to the Poisson fit with a ridge penalty that shrinks b towards equal shares 1 / n_ages, and if that also fails to the SVD estimates (method = "svd" with adjust = "dt"). Their forecasts are not those of the Poisson Lee-Carter model; wider age groups (mt_regroup()) or pooling (li_lee()) avoid them.

Draws describe the expected rates. Predictive draws (mt_forecast(predictive = TRUE)) add Poisson variation of the deaths given the rates and the exposures, the observation model of the Poisson Lee-Carter model (Brouhns, Denuit and Vermunt 2002); no other observation noise is added. If intervals are too narrow on real data, that is a property of the model: see recalibrated(), ensemble(), or overdispersed models such as family = "nb" below or stanmomo("lc", family = "nb") (stanmomo()).

Jump-off. The jump-off rates are the rates of the last year T of the fitting period, from which the forecast starts. Stoeldraijer et al. (2018) compare six options for the Lee-Carter model; their names are in quotes:

  • jump_off = "fitted": "model values", a[x] + b[x] k[T] (Lee and Carter 1992);

  • jump_off = "observed": "last observed values", the observed log rates of year T (Lee and Miller 2001): a[x] is replaced by them and k is 0 in year T;

  • jump_off = "observed", jump_off_years = n (n = 2 to 5 in the paper): "average n years observed". a[x] is the mean of the observed log rates of the last n years and k is 0 at the midpoint of these years; the random walk with drift carries the mean from the midpoint to year T, so the jump-off rates are that mean plus b[x] d (n - 1) / 2, with d the drift of k. The paper does not say how the index at the midpoint relates to the fitted index of year T; this reading (the forecast does not depend on k[T]) reproduces its results for French men (below), where the mean of the fitted index over the n years does not.

Stoeldraijer et al. call a forecast accurate if its out-of-sample errors in historical data are small (mean absolute error of life expectancy at 65 one and five years ahead), and robust if it changes little when one more year of data is added (standard deviation of the changes of the forecast life expectancy at 65 in 2020 between successive fitting periods). In eight Western European countries the last observed values were the most accurate for most countries and an average of observed years the most robust; more years averaged gave more robust and less accurate forecasts. For French men (Human Mortality Database in StanMoMo::FRMaleData, a later release than the paper's; ages 0-94 and 95+; fitting periods from 1960 to 2005, ..., 2014; method = "svd"), the mean absolute errors and the standard deviations of the last observed values and of the averages are within 0.03 years of Table 8a of the paper. Those of the model values differ by up to 0.08 years: the mean error of the fitted log rates at ages 65 and over in 2005-2014 is -0.002 with these data and 0.005 in the paper (Table 9a), and a shift of the log rates at these ages by 0.007 moves life expectancy at 65 by 0.05 years. anchored() moves the jump-off of any model.

Filtered jump-off (jump_off = "filtered"; De Jong and Tickle 2006). The paper writes the Lee-Carter model in state-space form (eq. 6): y[t] = a + b alpha[t] + eps[t] for the vector of log rates of year t, and alpha[t + 1] = delta + alpha[t] + lambda eta[t], with independent normal eps[t] (variance sigma^2 at every age) and eta[t] (variance sigma^2), b'b = 1 and the signal-to-noise ratio lambda. The forecast starts from a + b E(alpha[T] | y[1], ..., y[T]), the Kalman filter estimate of the index in the jump-off year (eq. 15). The paper estimates b and lambda by maximum likelihood with the Kalman filter, then a, delta and sigma given them (Section 5), for a model with B-spline age effects (eq. 2; eq. 6 is its case without splines, the model fitted here). Here a and b are those of the Lee-Carter fit (method), in the scale sum(b) = 1 of k; given them, sigma, lambda, delta and the level of the index in the first year are estimated by maximum likelihood of the paper's model for the observed log rates. The filtered index is computed in closed form (generalised least squares for the level and the drift and the best linear prediction of the index), which equals the Kalman filter with a diffuse initial state. Without state noise (lambda = 0, which is the estimate in some short or noisy series) it is the value in year T of the linear trend fitted to the per-year indices z[t] = b'(y[t] - a) / b'b; with little observation noise (large lambda) it approaches z[T], the projection of the observed log rates of year T on the age pattern, which is k[T] for method = "svd", adjust = "none". Only the start changes: the forecast keeps the drift and the innovations of k (the paper's forecast uses the maximum likelihood drift and adds the variance of the filtered index). Package-specific (reference unknown): cells without deaths enter with 0.5 deaths, as for jump_off = "observed"; age groups without deaths in the fitting period are left out; with bootstrap = TRUE each bootstrap fit filters the observed rates with its own a and b. mt_parameters() reports the filtered index (k_filtered), its standard error (se_k_filtered, which includes the uncertainty of the level and the drift) and the estimates filter_sigma, filter_lambda and filter_drift (per year, in the units of k). The paper's data (Australian women, 1921-2000) are not in an R package; tests check the limiting cases, a Kalman filter and recovery on simulated data.

Negative binomial version (family = "nb"; Delwarde, Denuit and Partrat 2007). Following the paper:

  • the deaths are negative binomial with mean mu = E exp(a[x] + b[x] k[t]) and variance mu + phi mu^2, a Poisson distribution mixed over a gamma distributed random effect of each cell (Section 2.2). The dispersion phi (the paper's k) is one parameter for all ages and years;

  • a, b, k and phi are estimated by maximum likelihood (eq. 5): uni-dimensional Newton updates of a, b and k (eq. 6-8), each given the other parameters, alternated with the estimate of phi given the fitted deaths;

  • k[t] follows a random walk with drift (Section 3.5);

  • predictive draws (mt_forecast(predictive = TRUE)) are negative binomial deaths with the estimated dispersion (size 1 / phi), the observation model of Section 2.2.

Package-specific (reference unknown): the Newton updates start from the Poisson estimates (the paper: a = 0, b = 1, k = 0, or random values); phi is maximised by Newton steps on log(phi) with step halving (the paper: Newton steps on 1 / phi, eq. 9); the estimate is 0 (the Poisson model) where the derivative of the log-likelihood at phi = 0 is not positive; the log-likelihood uses gamma functions, so deaths need not be whole numbers. The paper states no identification constraints; sum(b) = 1 and sum(k) = 0 of the Poisson model (Brouhns, Denuit and Vermunt 2002) agree with its Figures 2 and 3. As for the Poisson model, draws include the innovations of k and the uncertainty of its drift; the paper reports point forecasts only. With bootstrap = TRUE the resampled deaths are negative binomial with the estimated dispersion, and each draw has the dispersion of its bootstrap fit (package-specific). The ridge and SVD fallbacks are not used: a fit that does not converge fails. Like other maximum likelihood estimates of a variance, phi is biased downwards when many parameters are estimated relative to the number of cells. For France, ages 0-99, the fit to the Human Mortality Database series in demography::fr.mort reproduces the paper's dispersions (Section 3.3), AIC (Section 3.4) and drifts and standard deviations of k (Sections 3.5 and 3.6) within 1%; the paper's column labelled sigma^2 holds the standard deviation (divisor T - 1).

Dispersion by age (family = "nb" with dispersion = "age"; Li, Hardy and Tan 2009). Following the paper:

  • each cell consists of clusters whose deaths are Poisson given a gamma distributed frailty with mean 1 and a variance that depends on age. The deaths of the cell are then negative binomial with mean mu = E exp(a[x] + b[x] k[t]) and variance mu + alpha[x] mu^2 (Section 3, eq. 5-12), with one dispersion alpha[x] per age group of the data; alpha[x] near 0 gives the Poisson model;

  • a, b, k and alpha are estimated by maximum likelihood (eq. 13): the Newton updates of a, b and k of Appendix 1, alternated with the estimate of each alpha[x] given the fitted deaths of its age group;

  • jump_off = "constrained" applies the forecast origin correction (Section 3 and Appendix 2): a[x] is the observed log rate of the last year T (the paper writes a[x] = m[x, T]; a is on the log scale of eq. 1), k[T] = 0, and b and k are estimated by maximum likelihood under these constraints. The fitted rates of the last year are the observed ones, and the log-likelihood is lower than without the constraints (footnote 3). With family = "poisson" it gives the original model with the correction, which the paper fits for comparison (Section 4.2);

  • interval forecasts come from the parametric bootstrap of Section 3: bootstrap = TRUE simulates negative binomial deaths from the fitted model, re-estimates a, b and k (with jump_off = "constrained", a comes from the simulated deaths of the last year, as the correction is part of the estimation in Section 3), and simulates k from the time series model of each refit. The dispersions are those of the fit: step 2(a) re-estimates a, b and k. The paper's method is lee_carter(family = "nb", dispersion = "age", jump_off = "constrained", bootstrap = TRUE);

  • predictive draws (mt_forecast(predictive = TRUE)) are negative binomial deaths with the dispersion of their age group (size 1 / alpha[x]), the observation model of eq. (10). The paper's intervals describe the central death rates, which are the draws without predictive.

Package-specific (reference unknown): as for one dispersion, the updates start from the Poisson estimates (Appendix 1 recommends them), and each alpha[x] is maximised by Newton steps on log(alpha[x]) with step halving (the paper: Newton steps on alpha[x]). Its estimate is 0 where the derivative of the log-likelihood at 0 is not positive. The paper fits an ARIMA model to k without naming the model it chose; here k follows a random walk with drift, and the draws of each bootstrap fit include the uncertainty of its drift, as all draws of lee_carter(). With jump_off = "constrained", an age group without deaths in the last year starts from the rate of 0.5 deaths. Age groups without deaths in all years keep their constant rate and have Poisson deaths (dispersion 0). As with one dispersion, a fit that does not converge fails; jump_off = "constrained" has no fallbacks either. Each alpha[x] is estimated from cells that also estimate a[x], b[x] and k. Like other maximum likelihood estimates of a variance it is biased downwards: by about 2 / T with T years, and more at the ages that carry most of the information on k (many deaths and a small dispersion). The paper uses data of the Human Mortality Database for the United States and Canada, ages 0-99, 1950-2004 (Section 4.1). The packages demography and StMoMo do not hold these series, so its estimates are not reproduced.

rotate = TRUE rotates the age pattern of decline as life expectancy rises (Li, Lee and Gerland 2013; status: published, with the deviations listed below). In long-lived populations the decline of mortality slows down at young ages and speeds up at old ages, which a fixed b[x] does not capture over long horizons. For each path and year t, the life expectancy at birth e0 of the unrotated forecast gives the weight w = (0.5 (1 + sin(pi / 2 (2 u - 1))))^power with u = (e0 - e0_start) / (e0_end - e0_start); w is 0 below e0_start and 1 from e0_end (eq. 2 of the paper). The age pattern of that year is B[x, t] = (1 - w) b[x] + w bu[x] (eq. 3). The defaults are those of the paper: the rotation starts at 80 (about the median life expectancy of the 20 populations with the highest life expectancy in 2005-2010), is complete at 102 (the value with which the ratio of the death rates at age 0 and at ages 15-19 approaches its estimated long-run level of 7.7), and the exponent is 0.5. The ultimate pattern bu has the mean of b over ages 15-64 at all ages below 65, as in the paper. From age 65 it keeps the shape of b, scaled so that the first age group from 65 equals that mean, and it sums to 1 like b: the paper only notes that lowering b at young ages raises it at older ages because b sums to 1, and this scaling is that of MortCast (Sevcikova et al. 2016). The index is then solved again, path by path and year by year, so that the rotated rates have the same life expectancy at birth as the unrotated ones (eq. 4): rotation changes the age pattern of the forecast and keeps its life expectancy at birth. Decline thus moves from young ages to the ages where bu exceeds b. Where b at 65 is already above its mean over ages 15-64 (as for French women), it moves mostly to ages 15-64. Fitted rates, and paths with e0 below e0_start, are unchanged. Rotation needs ages from 0 (life expectancy at birth) with age groups starting at 15 and 65. With a closed last age group, a warning notes that life expectancy is then truncated at the highest age. Rotated forecasts compute life tables for every path and year and are much slower (about 20 times for single years of age).

Deviations of the rotation from Li, Lee and Gerland (2013):

  • the paper forecasts b and k for both sexes combined (Li and Lee 2005) and takes the weights from the life expectancy of both sexes combined; lee_carter() fits each stratum separately, so the weights come from the life expectancy of the stratum (MortCast takes the path of life expectancy from a separate model);

  • the paper illustrates the method with the median path of life expectancy; here every draw is rotated with its own path of life expectancy;

  • rates change from the jump-off year T, log m[x, t] = log m[x, T] + B[x, t] (k*[t] - k[T]). Eq. (4) writes a[x] + B[x, t] K[t] with a the last observed log rates (as jump_off = "observed") or their mean over the years; with jump_off = "fitted" (or "filtered") the fitted (or filtered) rates of year T are the starting point (package-specific), which keeps the jump-off rates when B departs from b;

  • the paper extends the open age group to age 130 with a logistic model before fitting (footnote 3); here the age groups of the data are used, and life expectancy closes the open interval with L = l / m (life_table()).

References

Lee RD, Carter LR (1992). Modeling and forecasting U.S. mortality. Journal of the American Statistical Association 87(419): 659-671.

Brouhns N, Denuit M, Vermunt JK (2002). A Poisson log-bilinear regression approach to the construction of projected lifetables. Insurance: Mathematics and Economics 31(3): 373-393. doi:10.1016/S0167-6687(02)00185-3

Booth H, Maindonald J, Smith L (2002). Applying Lee-Carter under conditions of variable mortality decline. Population Studies 56(3): 325-336. doi:10.1080/00324720215935

Lee R, Miller T (2001). Evaluating the performance of the Lee-Carter method for forecasting mortality. Demography 38(4): 537-549. doi:10.1353/dem.2001.0036

Stoeldraijer L, van Duin C, van Wissen L, Janssen F (2018). Comparing strategies for matching mortality forecasts to the most recently observed data: exploring the trade-off between accuracy and robustness. Genus 74: 16. doi:10.1186/s41118-018-0041-y

De Jong P, Tickle L (2006). Extending Lee-Carter mortality forecasting. Mathematical Population Studies 13(1): 1-18. doi:10.1080/08898480500452109

Delwarde A, Denuit M, Partrat C (2007). Negative binomial version of the Lee-Carter model for mortality forecasting. Applied Stochastic Models in Business and Industry 23(5): 385-401. doi:10.1002/asmb.679

Li JS-H, Hardy MR, Tan KS (2009). Uncertainty in mortality forecasting: an extension to the classical Lee-Carter approach. ASTIN Bulletin 39(1): 137-164. doi:10.2143/AST.39.1.2038060

Brouhns N, Denuit M, Van Keilegom I (2005). Bootstrapping the Poisson log-bilinear model for mortality forecasting. Scandinavian Actuarial Journal 2005(3): 212-224.

Renshaw AE, Haberman S (2008). On simulation-based approaches to risk measurement in mortality with specific reference to Poisson Lee-Carter modelling. Insurance: Mathematics and Economics 42(2): 797-816.

Li N, Lee R, Gerland P (2013). Extending the Lee-Carter method to model the rotation of age patterns of mortality decline for long-term projections. Demography 50(6): 2037-2051. doi:10.1007/s13524-013-0232-2

Li N, Lee R (2005). Coherent mortality forecasts for a group of populations: an extension of the Lee-Carter method. Demography 42(3): 575-594. doi:10.1353/dem.2005.0021

Sevcikova H, Li N, Kantorova V, Gerland P, Raftery AE (2016). Age-specific mortality and fertility rates for probabilistic population projections. In Schoen R (ed.) Dynamic Demographic Analysis. Springer, 285-310. doi:10.1007/978-3-319-26603-9_15

Examples

x <- mt_example(deaths = "single")
fit <- mt_fit(lee_carter(), x)
fc <- mt_forecast(fit, h = 10, n_draws = 200, seed = 1)
# \donttest{
# rotation needs ages from 0: French women (HMD, via demography)
if (requireNamespace("demography", quietly = TRUE)) {
  fr <- as_mt_data(demography::fr.mort, series = "female", years = 1970:2006)
  fr <- mt_regroup(fr, age = c(0, 1, seq(5, 100, 5)))
  fc_rot <- mt_forecast(mt_fit(lee_carter(rotate = TRUE), fr), h = 50, n_draws = 100, seed = 1)
  life_expectancy(fc_rot)
}

# negative binomial deaths (Delwarde, Denuit and Partrat 2007)
fit_nb <- mt_fit(lee_carter(family = "nb"), x)
mt_parameters(fit_nb)[parameter == "nb_dispersion"]
#>    stratum     parameter  index        value
#>     <char>        <char> <char>        <num>
#> 1:  female nb_dispersion        2.913877e-05
#> 2:    male nb_dispersion        0.000000e+00
# dispersion by age with the forecast origin correction and the parametric
# bootstrap (Li, Hardy and Tan 2009)
fit_lht <- mt_fit(lee_carter(family = "nb", dispersion = "age", jump_off = "constrained",
                             bootstrap = TRUE, n_boot = 20), mt_subset(x, sex == "female"))
mt_parameters(fit_lht)[parameter == "nb_dispersion"]

# jump-off: mean of the last three observed years (Stoeldraijer et al.
# 2018) and the Kalman filter estimate (De Jong and Tickle 2006)
fit_av <- mt_fit(lee_carter(jump_off = "observed", jump_off_years = 3), x)
fit_kf <- mt_fit(lee_carter(jump_off = "filtered"), x)
mt_parameters(fit_kf)[grepl("filter", parameter)]
